isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.answer: The four phases are preparation, detection and analysis, then containment, eradication and recovery, and finally post-incident activity. You contain first because cutting the machine off stops the attack spreading and stops the attacker controlling it. Cleaning while they are still active lets them come straight back. You leave a compromised machine powered on because its memory holds running processes and live connections, and that evidence is lost at power-off. A playbook is the written plan for one kind of incident, such as ransomware or a lost laptop. It lists concrete steps, each with an owner. The post-incident lessons-learned review feeds back into preparation, so the plan and playbooks get better after every incident.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::isc2.cc.d.answer: Worth logging: successful and failed sign-ins and where they came from, privilege changes such as new accounts or admin-group additions, configuration changes, access to sensitive data, and the security tools' own alerts. A SIEM collects logs from across the organisation and normalises them into one format. It then correlates events from different sources and raises alerts when a rule matches. Clocks must be synchronised to one time source, or events cannot be put in order. Logs must be sent to a separate store as they are written, so an intruder with admin rights cannot delete them. To investigate a brute-force attack, I would establish where the attempts came from, how many there were, which accounts were tried and over what time span. Then I would check whether any attempt from that source succeeded.
